item.title: Non-Monotonic Exciton Transport Efficiency in Multi-layer Ring-shaped Quantum Networks inspired by Photosystem I
item.description: arXiv:2610.13949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photosystem I (PSI) is one of the most efficient natural photosynthetic complexes and serves as a structural prototype for understanding excitation energy transfer (EET) and designing artificial light-harvesting systems. Here, we construct a multilayer elliptical-conical quantum network inspired by PSI to investigate how antenna architecture affects EET. Excitation dynamics are simulated using the quantum jump approach combined with coherent modified Redfield theory (QJA-CMRT). The transfer efficiency exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on pigment density, reaching a maximum of 0.86 at x=6 in the five-layer network. The optimal configuration contains 91 pigments, close to the number of core antenna pigments in natural PSI. Our combined density-of-states and kinetic analyses reveal that this nonmonotonic dependence originates from a trade-off: at low pigment densities, enhanced band overlap promotes energy transfer, whereas at high densities, excessive exciton delocalization compromises funnel directionality and reduces efficiency; the optimal configuration is consequently achieved at x=6. These findings provide insights into PSI antenna organization and offer guidelines for designing efficient artificial light-harvesting systems.
item.dc:creator: Yi Li, Rui Li, Kai-Ya Zhang, Ming-Zi Jin, Tao Liu, Qing Ai

item.title: Domain of Applicability of the Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA): A Critical Analysis for X-ray and Visible-Light Interface Scattering
item.description: arXiv:2610.14054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA) is established for X-ray interface scattering, yet its domain of applicability has never been stated explicitly. The DWBA implicitly rests on the small refractive index deviation (SRID) condition - satisfied by X-rays ($|n-1| \sim 10^{-6}$) but violated by visible light ($|n-1| \sim 0.5$). The DWBA mixes microscopic and macroscopic Maxwell equations, whereas a rigorous optical theory must be built on the macroscopic Maxwell equations and constitutive relations. Rigorous alternatives for two specific inconsistencies in the standard DWBA are discussed. The Extended Transfer Matrix Approach (ETMA) for visible-light interface scattering is outlined.
item.dc:creator: Reinhard Sigel

item.title: Partitioning the magnetization raises the stability limit of ferromagnetic colloids
item.description: arXiv:2610.14247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic actuation scales with a particle's magnetic moment, yet practical colloidal suspensions remain superparamagnetic or weakly magnetized, a permanent dipole drives a near contact attraction growing as the square of the moment, binding particles irreversibly. Here we show that this constraint depends not only on how much magnetic material a particle carries, but on where it sits. Partitioning a fixed moment M into N internal elements leaves the far field interaction, and every actuation force, unchanged while suppressing the near-field pair energy by 1/N. As we show in our experiments across 57 samples and three geometries, stability collapses onto a single $\sim M^{2}/N$ boundary, raising the accessible dipolar energy scale nearly 150-fold. A liquid-phase analogue of magnetic force microscopy images the engineered energy landscape directly. The resulting colloids outrun size-matched superparamagnetic beads in weak fields far from a magnetic source, suggesting their applicability in hard to reach places. Together, these results open a new operating regime for colloidal manipulation, with impactful implications in microfluidics and drug delivery.
item.dc:creator: Paramita Modak, Priyadharshini M, Ankur Jaiswar, Ambarish Ghosh

item.title: Explicit Solutions in a Probabilistic Cellular Automaton Model for Self-Assembled Monolayer Degradation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-assembled monolayers (SAMs), formed by the adsorption of a monomolecular layer of adsorbate onto a surface, have emerged as leading candidates for plat- forms for electrochemical biosensors. In order to characterize the working age of a SAM-based biosensor, it is necessary to understand the long-term degradation of the monolayer, with particular emphasis on the intermolecular forces present in the self-assembly process. In this work, discrete- and continuous-time proba- bilistic cellular automaton (PCA) models for the degradation of SAMs involving adsorbate-adsorbate interactions are proposed in which adsorbate molecules desorb at a rate dependent only on the number of adsorbed neighbors. Impor- tantly, we make no assumptions on the relationship between degradation rate and adsorbed neighbors. Using techniques from generating function theory and complex analysis, the expected degradation curve is solved for explicitly in one dimension and shown to be a sigmoid curve related to the Gompertz function.
item.dc:creator: Wes Caldwell, Ryan Evans, Jacob Majikes, Anthony Kearsley

item.title: Explicit Solvents Reverse Temperature Dependence of Phase Behavior in Charged Fluids
item.description: arXiv:2610.14366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In most theories of electrolyte and polyelectrolyte solutions, the solvent is treated implicitly as a dielectric continuum. While this approximation has enabled major advances, it neglects coupling between ionic and dipolar degrees of freedom. Using molecular dynamics simulations and the mean-spherical approximation, we show that this coupling qualitatively alters electrostatically driven phase behaviour. At finite ion concentrations, many-body ion-dipole correlations reverse the temperature dependence of effective electrostatic interactions, leading to upper-critical solution temperature (UCST) behaviour in direct contrast to the lower-critical solution temperature (LCST) behaviour predicted by implicit-solvent electrostatic theories. This phase reversal arises from ion-induced suppression of local dipolar screening, a collective effect inaccessible to pairwise implicit-solvent descriptions.
item.dc:creator: Pierre J. Walker, Zhen-Gang Wang

item.title: Biomolecular condensates and their pathologies: A colloidal, interfacial, and transport perspective
item.description: arXiv:2610.14398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biomolecular condensates are micron-scale, membraneless compartments that concentrate proteins and nucleic acids by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Condensates play critical roles in transcription, mRNA metabolism, stress responses, and signaling across the cell, with their dysregulation increasingly correlated with several pathologies spanning neurodegeneration, cancer, cardiometabolic disease, and viral infections. The emergent biology of condensates can be cohesively viewed through the framework of colloidal, interfacial, and transport phenomena. Here we review the condensate literature through this joint lens, treating each condensate as a biological colloid whose behavior is captured by four measurable physical quantities: a Flory--Huggins interaction parameter that determines whether the dense phase forms at all, a partition coefficient that dictates the degree of client molecule accumulation, a viscoelastic relaxation time that sets whether the dense phase responds as a liquid or a solid, and an interfacial tension that governs droplet shape and interfacial dynamics. Each quantity is traced to its physical origin, its measured range in biological condensates, and the techniques that quantify it, for both three-dimensional droplets and two-dimensional membrane-tethered condensates. Interpreting disease as the displacement of these physical quantities from their functional ranges, we reorganize condensate pathologies into a small set of physical failure modes --- saturation concentration dysregulation, aberrant aging and liquid-to-solid transitions, disrupted partitioning, interfacial aggregation, and pathogen hijacking --- and show how the same parameters become design variables for condensate-targeted drugs and engineered coacervate delivery vehicles. The review concludes with open questions at the interface of condensate biology and colloidal and interfacial science.
item.dc:creator: Vineeth Godavarti, Vinny Chandran Suja

item.title: Soft-to-Rigid: Shape Continuation as an Alternative Search for Packing Congruent Shapes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Searches for dense packings of congruent shapes move rigid pieces. Hardening starts each piece as its inscribed disk and deforms it into the target shape while the container is compressed. We ask whether it is a search worth running alongside existing ones, and test it at matched budget and comparable tuning against rigid starts, growth, simulated annealing and perturbation--compression on seven families of squares, triangles, hexagons and disks in squares, triangles and circles (188 instances), scoring each method by the lowest container size it reaches. Hardening is not a better default: tuned rigid starts reach the lowest size most often. It is a different search. On squares in a square it reaches packings the other four methods miss, including Trump's n = 11 and Wainwright's n = 19 in 32 runs per method, and in a targeted follow-up campaign at ten times the budget (16 runs per method) it is the only one to reach the best known packings for n = 17 and n = 26, while annealing alone reaches n = 27. In exploratory ablations, compressing disks and then switching to polygons at once, or growing rigid polygons along hardening's area schedule, shows no detectable difference from rigid starts, and hardening's unique packings contain more tilted pieces. The bias costs elsewhere: hardening is worse on triangles and on four families held out from all development, where the short-pilot policy we tested showed no detected advantage over always starting rigid. Shape continuation is an alternative search that reaches different packings, worth keeping beside rigid ones; we did not show that splitting a fixed budget between them pays, and we have no test that predicts where it helps. Search campaigns were planned before they ran, with amendments, exploratory analyses and post-hoc checks identified separately; every run is replayable and every number is generated from an event log.
item.dc:creator: Yohei Nakajima

item.title: Optoelectronically Enabled Simultaneous and Decoupled Navigation and Selective Pairing of Electrically Driven Janus Particles for Multi-Agent Microrobotics
item.description: arXiv:2610.14560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-propelled Janus particles are promising active agents for microscale manipulation and microrobotic applications. However, when powered by a global external energy source, such as an electric, magnetic, or optical field, all particles respond simultaneously, preventing their independent and concurrent control. Achieving parallel, decoupled control without continuous particle-specific feedback, while preserving intrinsic self-propulsion, remains a significant challenge. Here, we present an optoelectronic (OE) strategy for simultaneously and independently controlling electrically driven, self-propelled metallo-dielectric Janus particles (JPs) using spatially programmable virtual electrodes. These electrodes are generated by projecting a single predefined illumination pattern from a digital micromirror device onto a photoconductive surface. The resulting confinement landscape enables multiple JPs to follow distinct trajectories without continuous monitoring, feedback, or pattern reconfiguration. We demonstrate controlled pairing of JPs with passive polystyrene particles and biological cells. For automated multi-agent operation, an image-based assignment framework identifies optimal agent-target pairs, excludes intersecting trajectories, and generates a single composite pattern for simultaneous, selective pair formation without real-time updating. Finally, we demonstrate independent manipulation of multiple magnetically rolling JPs under a globally applied magnetic field. Overall, this programmable open-loop strategy provides a versatile framework for multi-agent microrobotic manipulation, with potential applications in in-vitro micromanipulation and microfluidic systems.
item.dc:creator: Srikanta Debata, Ido Rachbuch, Gilad Yossifon

item.title: Surface Granular flows: Two Related Examples
item.description: arXiv:2610.14592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Granular surface flows are common in industrial practice and natural systems, however, theoretical description of such flows is at present incomplete. Two prototype systems involving surface flow are compared: heap formation by pouring at a point and rotating cylinders. Continuum models for analysis of these flows are reviewed, and experimental results for quasi-2d systems are presented. Experimental results in both systems are well described by continuum models.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Advances in Complex Systems, Vol. 4, No. 4 (2001) 407-417
item.dc:creator: Devang V. Khakhar, Ashish V. Orpe

item.title: Active remodeling rescues a microswimmer from geometric trapping
item.description: arXiv:2610.14805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural habitats confront microorganisms with heterogeneous, mechanically complex surroundings that shape how they move and explore. Most studies of motility in complex media treat the environment as either a homogeneous fluid or a rigid obstacle field. Here we instead study a medium that is simultaneously soft and reconfigurable --- deformable by the organism moving through it. We track the unicellular biflagellate microalga \emph{Chlamydomonas reinhardtii} swimming in a soft, disordered suspension of microgel particles comparable in size to the cell itself, across a range of gel packing fractions. With increasing packing fraction, trajectories change from long straight runs to short, frequently reorienting ones, and the effective translational diffusivity decreases monotonically. The bimodal run/tumble speed distribution, characteristic of the free-swimming gait, collapses toward a single mode as the packing fraction increases, by near-proportional slowing of both gait states rather than a redistribution of cells between them. Recasting trajectories as alternating hops and traps reveals the signature of a deformable medium: hop lengths halve as the gel densifies, approaching the microgel aggregate scale, while trapping times do not increase with increasing packing fraction. Independent force estimates place the cell's propulsive force close to an order of magnitude above that needed to deform a single grain, so remodeling is expected rather than merely observed. A minimal \emph{active remodeler} model --- an active Brownian particle among mobile, rigid obstacles --- shows that obstacle mobility alone is sufficient to relocate the onset of permanent trapping. Thus, our results establish obstacle mobility as a control parameter for motility in soft, disordered matter.
item.dc:creator: Ayushi Bhatt, Nico Schramma, Jasper van der Gucht, Uddalok Sen

item.title: A Higher-Order Stroh Framework for Weakly Nonlinear Post-Bifurcation Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.14869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear stability analysis predicts the onset of wrinkling, while weakly nonlinear analysis determines whether the bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical through the sign of the cubic amplitude coefficient. When this coefficient vanishes, higher-order terms are needed. In this paper, we develop a higher-order Stroh framework for weakly nonlinear post-bifurcation analysis of finitely deformed elastic solids. For each nonzero harmonic, the same base-state Stroh operator is retained at every order, with nonlinear source terms assembled from lower-order fields to account for geometry, constitutive laws and constraints. This recursive structure, together with Fredholm solvability conditions, enables us to derive cubic, quintic and higher-order amplitude equations. Here, we demonstrate the power of this framework by analysing wrinkling in an incompressible neo-Hookean film bonded to an exponentially graded substrate. The results recover established linear instability benchmarks and the supercritical-subcritical transition in the homogeneous-substrate limit. For graded substrates, the cubic coefficient vanishes on a surface in the parameter space of modulus ratio and substrate gradation. On this surface, the quintic coefficient takes both signs, corresponding to supercritical and subcritical bifurcations. These regions are separated by a curve along which the quintic coefficient also vanishes. Determining the branch direction along this curve requires higher-order terms, which can be calculated within the same framework.
item.dc:creator: Shiyuan Deng, Han Ye, Yafei Wang, Lizichen Chen, Alain Goriely, Yibin Fu, Weiqiu Chen, Chaofeng L\"u, Michel Destrade, Kecheng Li, Yangkun Du

item.title: A Minimal Theoretical Model for Morphodynamic Selection in Soft Matter Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.14967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Soft matter systems often display shape transitions, mode competition, and threshold-like dynamical responses driven by the coupling between mechanics, geometry, and biochemical or active fields. Here we present a minimal theoretical framework for describing such morphodynamic selection using a small number of physically interpretable order parameters. The model combines elastic relaxation, active driving, and nonlinear feedback, yielding distinct regimes corresponding to weak deformation, single-mode selection, and coupled shape transformation. We derive the governing equations, identify the relevant dimensionless control parameters, and show how the phase behavior can be organized in terms of threshold competition and effective coupling strengths. The framework provides a compact route for connecting analytical theory, numerical simulations, and experimentally observable shape dynamics in soft and biological matter.
item.dc:creator: Weihua Mu, Da Wang

item.title: Time-temperature-composition equivalence of the viscoelastic behavior through the glass transition of digitally mixed 3D-printed polymers
item.description: arXiv:2610.14986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The linear viscoelastic behavior of a polymer shows an equivalence of loading frequency and temperature, the time-temperature equivalence (TTE). Horizontal shifting extends moduli measured over limited ranges to much wider ranges, through the glass transition. Multimaterial 3D printing has created digitally mixed polymers, a new class in which elastomeric and glassy resins are mixed voxel by voxel in prescribed ratios. Composition shifts the location and breadth of the glass transition and increases the rubbery modulus. Here we extend TTE to a time-temperature-composition equivalence (TTCE). Across all measured temperatures, frequencies, and compositions, the storage modulus collapses onto one master curve. Composition translates the transition and stretches its breadth, both linearly. The phase angle and relaxation spectrum superpose under the same operations, so the family shares one distribution of relaxation times. A single closed-form TTCE gives the storage and loss moduli of the family, guiding graded and architected designs for elasticity and dissipation.
item.dc:creator: Beijun Shen, Sanat K. Kumar, Mary C. Boyce

item.title: Contact-mediated asymmetric delay and rate memory in snapping beam pairs
item.description: arXiv:2610.15119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Slender structures in dense environments interact through contact, which alters how and when they become unstable. Here we show that contact makes snap-through history dependent, so that when and whether a beam pair snaps depends on how long the contact is loaded. Under cyclic compression, the pair snaps on loading, snaps on unloading, or stays packed, with the loading and unloading rates selecting among the three. Upon contact, one beam rolls along the other without slip, and faster driving lets it roll further before it slides and snaps: to larger compression on loading and to smaller compression on unloading. This delay is asymmetric between loading and unloading as the unloading branch carries a memory of the loading rate. Interestingly, above a threshold compression the pair snaps even when the compression is stopped, with the time to snap diverging at that threshold. By exploiting this asymmetric, rate-dependent delay, we program ordered sequences of snap events in arrays of pairs with tunable gaps, and demonstrate that the energy dissipated per cycle becomes a two-parameter function of the loading and unloading rates, increasing fourfold when, at the fastest loading, the return is slowed.
item.dc:creator: Gavin Linton, Shima Mahmoudirad, Nidhi Pashine, Anupam Pandey

item.title: Reparameterizing GFN1-xTB for Ionic Liquids
item.description: arXiv:2610.15190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ionic liquids are materials whose properties can be tailored for a wide range of applications, but their chemical diversity and complex electronic structure make systematic screening using quantum-mechanical methods computationally demanding. Semiempirical quantum methods offer an alternative, although their accuracy depends on their parameterization. We investigate the reparameterization of the DFTB method GFN1-xTB for predicting structural, energetic, and electronic properties of ionic liquids. For this purpose, we built a database containing over 14,000 conformations to construct training datasets and explored different parameterization strategies fitted to binding energies, forces, HOMO-LUMO gaps, and geometries. Analysis of the original GFN1-xTB model reveals systematic errors in these properties, with distinct behavior for saturated and aromatic cations. Thus, we investigate two models: CXMIM-xTB, a targeted model trained on imidazolium-based ionic liquids, and IL-xTB, a more general model designed to describe systems containing saturated and aromatic cations. CXMIM-xTB improves the description of binding energies, geometries, and frontier orbital energies while retaining computational efficiency. The model is subsequently applied to estimate electrochemical windows of ionic liquids, providing values consistent with DFT and experimental values. IL-xTB follows a hierarchical parameterization strategy including different cation and anion families and substantially reduces the systematic errors of GFN1-xTB across the chemical space considered, providing a route for developing xTB parameterizations with broader applicability to ionic liquids. Overall, both parameterization strategies outperform the original GFN1-xTB model, demonstrating that reparameterized methods provide an efficient approach for connecting configurational sampling with quantum-mechanical properties of ionic liquids.
item.dc:creator: F. Stavarache, S. Calero, J. M. Vicent-Luna

item.title: Generalized Constraint-Controlled Rheological Model: Two Constitutive Pathways under Sinusoidal Periodic Shear Deformation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate the Generalized Constraint-Controlled Rheological Model (GCCRM) for entangled linear and long-arm-branched polymer melts under sinusoidal periodic shear deformation (SPSD), spanning the linear and strongly nonlinear regimes. Molecular architecture, conformation, chain stretch, flow-active constraints, convective constraint release, dynamic tube dilation, and activated arm retraction define a common upstream molecular state. This state feeds two time-domain constitutive pathways (a configurational stress and a dissipative internal-variable stress) which are recombined before Fourier analysis. For branched polymers, the architecture is described by an entire backbone of molecular weight $M_{bb}$ and $N_a$ long arms of molecular weight $M_a$, with a compliance-weighted representative-constitutive-cell partition. The linear limit is normalized so that the configurational moduli sum to the entanglement modulus, while dynamic tube dilation and stretch drive distinct contributions to dissipative activation. Under reduced closures, GCCRM generates a smooth nonlinear elastic response with an onset of nonlinearity, an approximately logarithmic growth regime, an architecture-dependent maximum, and distinct high-deformation asymptotes. Fourier harmonics, ELR, VLR, and Lissajous curves are treated as post-processing observables of the total stress. The framework establishes a consistent constitutive architecture whose quantitative validation requires one parameter set per material across SPSD and, prospectively, transient shear histories.
item.dc:creator: Dario Nichetti, Alessio Zaccone

item.title: Unlocking the potential of polymer networks for high strength through topology
item.description: arXiv:2610.15552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A covalent polymer network is orders of magnitude weaker than individual covalent bonds. This large gap reveals an unrealized potential. The weakness of a network comes not from individual covalent bonds, but from how they are connected. Here we unlock this potential by identifying a topological criterion, involving optimally sparse crosslinks, long chains, and dense entanglements. Optimizing each topological variable alone is insufficient for high strength, yet exceptional strength emerges when they are combined within a narrow regime. We describe the physics of this synergy, and use the criterion to strengthen networks widely used but known to be weak. For example, we prepare a polyacrylamide hydrogel of 90 wt% water, amplifying strength from a commonly reported value of ~0.1 MPa to ~6.5 MPa. The exceptional strength is achieved without sacrificing other properties, such as softness, toughness, and elasticity. The criterion establishes topology as a general design principle for strong polymer networks.
item.dc:creator: Zheqi Chen, Yu Zhou, Chenghai Li, Ho Cheung Shum, Zhigang Suo

item.title: Emergence of Active Foams in a Minimal Cognitive Flocking Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.15835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a minimal visual perception-driven model of self-propelled particles that interact through purely position-based cohesive steering within a finite vision cone, in the absence of velocity alignment and physical volume exclusion. Building on a previously proposed minimal cognitive model, we extend the interaction range from the previously studied short-range and distance-independent limits to an intermediate regime, enabling a systematic investigation of how a finite vision range influences collective behavior. We find that this regime exhibits a rich state diagram that combines characteristics of both limiting cases while giving rise to qualitatively new collective states. Besides the gas, nematic-band, and polar file states, we uncover the emergence of \emph{active foams} -- system-spanning fractal-like networks sustained by dynamically evolving particle streams. These structures arise solely from non-reciprocal vision-based interactions and are absent in both the short and long vision-range limits. For larger vision angles, the system self-organizes into a variety of aggregate morphologies, including condensates, rings, and multi-twist filaments, revealing a strong interplay between interaction range and anisotropic perception in shaping collective organization.
item.dc:creator: Aryan Dwivedi, Diganta Bhaskar, Anil Kumar Dasanna

item.title: Spreading the Damage: How Heterogeneity Delocalizes Fracture in Polymer Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.15962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fracture in polymer networks is strongly influenced by how network architecture and topology organize damage in space. Although these materials can sustain large deformations under homogeneous loading, they often fail in a brittle and flaw-sensitive manner once defects are present. Here we show that network heterogeneity is one key architectural parameter controlling this transition. Using a discrete mesoscale network model that explicitly resolves strand-level prestretch, force transmission, and irreversible bond scission, we demonstrate that heterogeneity in prestretch and strand lengths broadens crack-induced deformation, delocalizes bond rupture, and enlarges the fracture process zone. In polydisperse networks, increasing contour-length disorder broadens the prestretch distribution and systematically increases both toughness and the intrinsic length scale governing flaw sensitivity. Bimodal networks amplify this mechanism further through combined contrasts in prestretch and strand lengths, producing the largest damage zones and the highest toughness among the architectures studied. Inspired by the results, we derive a scaling estimate relating the emergent fracture-active length to the spatial range of crack-induced deformation and the logarithmic spread of strands' remaining stretch to rupture.
item.dc:creator: Saleh Assadi, Zachary White, Radhika Joshi, Franck J. Vernerey

item.title: Molecular-Level Evaluation of the Thermodynamic Properties of Charged Solutions from Submolar to Molar Ion Concentrations
item.description: arXiv:2610.15985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The accurate estimation of the ionic activity coefficients is paramount for the characterization of the electrochemical reactions driving energy storage processes as well as the biological mechanisms involving ATP hydrolysis. The numerical evaluation of the ionic activity coefficients by computational methods is rendered difficult by the infinite dilution limit involved in the integral identity between the Helmholtz free energy and the equation of state of the electrolyte. By combining a recently introduced self-consistent Debye-Huckel formalism and its analytically tractable low density limit, we develop a computationally efficient approach enabling the accurate calculation of the free energy and the related thermodynamic functions of aqueous electrolytes over a broad range of ionic concentration and electrostatic coupling strength. Via comparison with numerical simulations and experimental data, it is shown that our approach can predict the salt dependence of the Helmholtz free energy, the entropy, and the ionic activity coefficients from the electrostatically driven submolar ion concentrations to the hard-core dominated molar density regime.
item.dc:creator: Sahin Buyukdagli

item.title: Deformation-induced spectral softening drives phase separation on non-spherical membranes
item.description: arXiv:2610.16037v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Models of curvature-driven membrane sorting couple composition directly to membrane bending elasticity. Here we show that shape deformations can destabilize a homogeneous state without this composition-dependent mechanical coupling. We analyze the eigenspectrum of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on deformed spheres analytically, and verify it numerically. As the deformation amplitude increases, the spectral degeneracy breaks, and the lowest nonzero eigenvalue decreases substantially. Using Cahn-Hilliard dynamics, we show that this eigenvalue softening provides a purely geometric route to phase separation.
item.dc:creator: Avraham Moriel, Howard A. Stone

item.title: Length-scale dependence of collective time reparameterization in swap dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.16168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Swap Monte Carlo dramatically accelerates the equilibration of deeply supercooled liquids while preserving the equilibrium Boltzmann distribution. Recent work has argued that swap and other accelerated algorithms act by reparameterizing time: different dynamics follow the same slow relaxation process, but with different clocks. Here we test this idea in a continuously polydisperse glass former. We confirm that mean collective overlaps satisfy an approximate time reparameterization, in agreement with earlier results. However, the associated clock depends systematically on the collective probe length and on the relaxation stage. Thus the observed collective collapse does not define a unique, observable-independent material time. Over the numerically accessible $\alpha$-relaxation regime, swap changes not only the rate of relaxation, but also its length-scale dependence. The resulting collective reparameterization is therefore only approximate and does not establish an exact dynamical equivalence between swap and reference relaxation.
item.dc:creator: Massimo Pica Ciamarra

item.title: Self-Avoidance Governs Re-entrant Coil-Globule Transition of Inertial Active Brownian Ring Polymers
item.description: arXiv:2610.16188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active matter systems composed of self-propelled entities exhibit a wide range of out-of-equilibrium phase behaviors and collective dynamics. Assemblies of active particles, e.g., in a linear structure, are particularly interesting, as they exhibit an intriguing interplay between activity and geometrical restrictions due to self-avoidance and entanglements. Using Langevin dynamics simulations of an active Brownian ring polymer with translational and rotational inertia, we uncover an inertia-driven re-entrant coil-globule transition in the absence of any attractive interactions. We show that rotational inertia plays a paramount role, leading, in the globular state, to spontaneous, nonzero, radially outward polarization of the active forces. Self-avoidance and entanglements break the rotational symmetry of active beads and effectively stabilize the globular states. The transition becomes increasingly sharp with increasing rotational inertia, yielding highly compact globular conformations at intermediate activities, whereas at high activity the polymer re-expands into a coil state. Scaling of the radius of gyration reveals crossovers from self-avoiding, phantom-like to compact-globular structures. Further, rotational inertia enhances transport properties, with an intermediate activity-induced Rouse-type bead diffusion and a long-time diffusion coefficient displaying a power-law dependence on the moment of inertia. Our study establishes a purely inertia-induced mechanism for controlling the collapse of active polymers, arising from spontaneous active-force polarization and self-avoidance.
item.dc:creator: Rakesh Palariya, Arindam Panda, Roland G. Winkler, Sunil P Singh

item.title: Defining Thixotropy
item.description: arXiv:2610.16237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Originally coined 100 years ago to represent a shear-reversible sol-gel transition, the range of the term "thixotropy" has gradually expanded to encompass time-dependent changes in viscosity. Since this risks confusing "thixotropy" with ordinary nonlinear viscoelastic behavior, in this work we seek simple, historically faithful, quantifiable, and experimentally testable definitions of "thixotropy" that avoid this confusion. By analysing both historical tradition and published experimental data, we arrive at three complementary definitions. Definition 0 provides an idealized, purely inelastic reference useful primarily for recognizing thixotropy in a constitutive equation. Definitions 1 and 2, which are more practical, require, respectively, unusually large strains to reach steady state, and unbounded growth of the material relaxation time during rest. Definition 1 can apply in either shear-rate or stress-controlled modes, with the latter encompassing the so-called "viscosity bifurcation." These criteria are tested across diverse materials that we identify as thixotropic based on their responses clearly exceeding their viscoelastic reference scales. The framework is deliberately phenomenological and does not require specific microscopic mechanisms, allowing diverse materials to be described within a common rheological language, as is typical for rheological terminology. We believe that these definitions provide a practical framework for assigning thixotropy a more definite place in rheological taxonomy.
item.dc:creator: Yogesh M. Joshi, Ronald G. Larson

item.title: Dynamical-state switching controls active microrod navigation in porous media
item.description: arXiv:2610.16331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive search and travel strategies enable biological swimmers to explore complex environments, but remain difficult to encode in minimal synthetic microswimmers. Here, we unveil multiple dynamical and orientational states of rod-like Janus microswimmers actuated via electric fields: planar active, oriented chiral and persistent rods. We discover a hidden dynamical state after pre-orienting them, which allows us to switch on demand from strong chiral to persistent motion. We harness this phenomenological orientation and chirality switch for exploration in microstructured porous arrays. Here, strong chirality promotes local scanning but drives circular trapping and poor net displacement, whereas the pre-aligned dynamical state enables efficient obstacle sorting, and trap escape. Comparing experiments with simulations of active Brownian particles in the very same experimentally-extracted obstacle geometries, we quantify navigation efficiency via first-passage time statistics, revealing how chirality tuning optimizes the trade-off between local exploration and long-range transport.
item.dc:creator: Ana Cazorla, Maria L. Jimenez, Raul A. Rica-Alarcon, Carla Fernandez-Rico, Laura Alvarez

item.title: Derjaguin-corrected Kelvin equation for finite open slits
item.description: arXiv:2610.16367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate a Derjaguin-corrected Kelvin equation for phase transitions in finite open slits. In such pores, capillary condensation is modified by the finite wall length because the condensed phase is bounded by two terminal menisci pinned at the slit ends. Starting from the macroscopic generalized Kelvin equation, we introduce a scaling approximation which replaces the implicit edge-contact-angle condition by a closed analytic expression while preserving the exact limiting behaviours. We then incorporate mesoscopic wetting-layer contributions into the finite-slit free-energy balance. The single-wall contribution naturally separates into a planar Derjaguin term and a residual finite-length correction controlled by the competition between the wall length $H$ and the parallel correlation length $\xi_\parallel$. The resulting equation reduces to the standard Derjaguin-Kelvin equation for infinitely long slits and to the macroscopic finite-slit Kelvin equation when adsorbed layers are absent. Explicit forms are derived for long-ranged dispersion forces and for short-ranged forces. The theory is tested using classical density functional theory for finite slits with attractive Lennard-Jones walls and hard walls, corresponding respectively to capillary condensation and its drying analogue, capillary evaporation. The Derjaguin-corrected theory substantially improves on the purely macroscopic prediction, capturing both the correct infinite-slit limit and the observed dependence on wall length. For the short-ranged hard-wall system, the agreement with DFT remains nearly quantitative even for very narrow slits.
item.dc:creator: Alexandr Malijevsk\'y

item.title: Thermal softening of the yield stress in glasses with different stability
item.description: arXiv:2610.16424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The yielding of amorphous solids has been extensively studied in the athermal limit, but the influence of thermal fluctuations is much less understood, in particular for glasses of different stability. Using molecular dynamics simulations of a model glass where the swap Monte Carlo algorithm can be employed, we study the yield stress at finite temperature and shear rate, both in steady flow and at shear start-up, over a broad range of glass stability. Thermal fluctuations soften both the dynamic yield stress in steady state and the start-up yield stress. In all cases, the temperature dependence is compatible with the $T^{2/3}$ law expected for thermally activated yielding near a saddle-node instability, with no systematic dependence of the exponent on stability or shear rate. Extrapolations to zero temperature recover the athermal yield stresses. The amplitude of the softening at start-up, by contrast, depends strongly on stability: highly stable glasses are much less sensitive to temperature than poorly annealed ones. A description of yielding at finite temperature must therefore account explicitly for the stability of the glass.
item.dc:creator: Tianze Wan, Ludovic Berthier

item.title: Activity-Induced Structural and Dynamical Heterogeneity in Colloidal Gels
item.description: arXiv:2610.16553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active gels are intrinsically non-equilibrium materials whose structural and dynamical heterogeneity emerges from the interplay of attractive interactions, thermal fluctuations, and self-propulsion. We investigate a model active gel, simulated using large-scale Brownian dynamics simulations, to explore the effects of temperature $T$, active force strength $f_0$, persistence timescale $\tau_p$, and active particle concentration $\rho_a$. We characterize the structure of the evolving gel network through morphological analysis, while dynamical changes are quantified by the relaxation timescale and dynamical heterogeneity (DH). We show that an optimal choice of activity parameters yields a percolating gel network with faster gelation and larger voids and clusters, enhancing mechanical stability. Conversely, the structural relaxation timescale and DH decrease with increasing activity, indicating enhanced particle rearrangements and reduced spatial correlations of mobile and immobile regions. An effective temperature ($T_\text{eff}$) framework for colloidal gels maps structural quantities and relaxation timescales in an active gel onto those of a passive gel. More interestingly, the growth of DH with increasing swim force can also be described by the same effective-temperature framework, in stark contrast to observations in active glasses. Our findings show that, in colloidal gels, temperature and active force compete, giving rise to similar structural ordering and, consequently, similar DH at the same $T_\text{eff}$. These findings highlight the crucial role of structural ordering in governing DH in active colloidal gels, as compared to active glasses.
item.dc:creator: Santu Nath, Sudipta Mandal, Smarajit Karmakar

item.title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.16599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Poorly soluble species can have mean populations below one in small systems such as nanopores. In this regime, the grand-potential minimum, which identifies the most probable particle number, differs from the ensemble-averaged solute loading. We use grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling (GCWLS) to calculate the density of states $\Omega(N_\mathrm{A}, N_\mathrm{B})$ for a binary Lennard-Jones mixture of solute B in solvent A, both in bulk and in slit pores. One set of GCWLS simulations gives ensemble averages over a range of chemical potentials, whereas conventional grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation requires a separate simulation at each state point. Independent GCMC simulations confirm the GCWLS ensemble averages. The solvent number distribution is nearly Gaussian, whereas the dilute solute distribution is skewed and Poisson-like. The most probable solute number therefore lies below the ensemble-averaged loading $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle$ and is zero whenever $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle<1$. Reading the solute loading from the grand-potential minimum underestimates it and can falsely indicate that no solute is present. Defining the oversolubility as $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}=x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}/x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$, where $x_\mathrm{B}$ is the solute mole fraction, we find $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}\approx12$ in a pore of 3.5 particle diameters width when both wall interactions are repulsive. Adding wall-solute attraction moderately raises it to $\approx13$, whereas wall-solvent attraction lowers it to $\approx3.4$. This comparison shows that the wall-solvent interaction controls most of the enhancement. As the pore widens, $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}$ decreases toward unity. In bulk and in nanopores alike, the solubility of poorly soluble species should be obtained from ensemble averages rather than from grand-potential minima.
item.dc:creator: Russell Kajouri, Adyant Agrawal, Philipp St\"ark, Alexander Schlaich, Christian Holm

item.title: Colloid-Colloid Interactions Impact Network Morphology of Confined Colloidal Drying Patterns
item.description: arXiv:2610.16695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Colloidal suspensions that are confined between two closely spaced plates and left to evaporate slowly form maze-like labyrinth patterns in the final stage of evaporation. The fingers in these patterns form bifurcations and occasionally loops, which we may quantify with a skeletonization method. We compare drying patterns formed with two different salt concentrations in the droplet which changes the screening length and therefore the effective colloid interactions. We find that the junctions generally follow Murray's law for optimal transport networks, and that the typical bifurcation angles peak around 53. Screened droplets additionally show more loopy networks, and is characterized by bands of transversal fingers before merging into a central non-fingering colloidal aggregate. Our observations suggest that colloid-colloid interactions can strongly influence the large-scale topology of the pattern while leaving the local geometry of the individual fingers unchanged.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Andersen Hennig, Natalia Kizilova, Ilaria Beechey-Newman, Erika Eiser

item.title: Impact of shear and dilational membrane viscosities on capsule shape and dynamics under shear flow: a theoretical study
item.description: arXiv:2610.16739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In artificial (micro)capsules or cells such as red blood cells for example, the two-dimensional (2D) rheology of the membrane (or the shell) is viscoelastic and not only elastic. The deformation and inclination of such a capsule are theoretically studied under shear and extensional flows. The membrane mechanics is described by the Kelvin-Voigt model: the 2D dissipation with the Boussinesq-Scriven law associated to specific dilational and shear Boussinesq numbers $Bq_d$ and $Bq_d$ respectively while the elastic constitutive law is either Hookean, strain-softening (neoHookean) or strain-hardening (Skalak). The dynamics depends on the elastic capillary number $Ca$, the Poisson ratio (or $C$ in Skalak law), the viscosity ratio $\lambda$, the nonlinearities included in the constitutive law and both boussinesq numbers. Three dynamics are identified in the limit of weak deformations: a tank-treading motion in the limit of small elastic capillary number with a characteristic time depending on $\lambda$, $Bq_s$ and $Bq_d$, an oscillation without any elasticity and a damped oscillation leading to a tank-treading motion in the limit of large Boussinesq numbers. In all cases, both shear and dilational 2D dissipations contribute differently leading to non-trivial results. In the case of a Skalak law with $C=1$, $Bq=Bq_s=Bq_d$ and $Bq>>\lambda$, the deformations in the limits $Ca<<1$, $Bq=O(1)$ and $Ca=O(1)$, $Bq>>1$ determined in the seminal work of \cite{barthes1985role} are recovered.
item.dc:creator: Paul Regazzi, Marc Leonetti

item.title: Self-phoresis on a one-dimensional periodic domain
item.description: arXiv:2610.16791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the spontaneous motion and collective dynamics of self-phoretic particles on a one-dimensional periodic domain. The particles act as localized chemical sources (of a particle-dependent strength) of a field and the particles themselves respond to the gradients of the field they generate (with a particle-dependent phoretic mobility). The chemical field itself diffuses and evaporates. For a single particle, we derive the exact threshold for spontaneous propulsion and establish the emergence of stable constant-velocity states near onset through a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation. We then consider an active source coupled to a non-emitting tracer and determine the conditions for slipping and stable phase-locked motion. For two mutually coupled sources, the stationary antipodal configuration can lose stability through either a pitchfork or a Hopf bifurcation, depending on the relative source strengths and phoretic mobilities. We determine the competing instability thresholds and compare them with direct numerical simulations of the coupled particle-field equations. Beyond onset, the resulting translating and oscillatory states provide qualitative counterparts to modes of motion observed experimentally for camphor disks in annular water channels. These results connect the onset of individual propulsion, tracer entrainment, and collective motion within a common analytically tractable framework.
item.dc:creator: Leah Anderson, David S. Dean

item.title: First-fracture kinetics in periodic chains: from free-energy landscapes and dynamical recrossing to absolute rates
item.description: arXiv:2610.16944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The nearly collinear configuration of highly stretched polymer chains before fracture motivates one-dimensional models. At fixed extension, stretching one bond redistributes length among the others, coupling rupture to the whole chain. In this work, I develop a framework for fracture-healing rates in periodic Morse chains, combining deterministic theories, equilibrium simulations and a quasi-deterministic approach using equilibrium fluxes and barrier-top trajectories. Constrained-partition calculations closely reproduce simulated populations and intact-state tensions. An intact-reservoir potential of mean force (PMF) supplies the first-fracture surface probability, while recrossing corrects the attempt flux without a rate-fitted prefactor. Independent rate tests identify an operational chain-length boundary for accurate two-state kinetics; failed-return durations decrease relative to population relaxation as chains grow. Kramers-Grote-Hynes (KGH), nonlinear reactive-flux and equilibrium rates show excellent agreement in this regime. KGH predicts rates away from coexistence and a chain-dependent local activation length dominated by the barrier response. Rates decrease approximately exponentially before declining more gently for longer chains: barrier growth dominates, additional fracture sites partly compensate, and transmission varies more weakly. Beyond coexistence, long chains can fracture practically irreversibly because healing becomes too rare to observe. Projected committor crossings, where the configuration-averaged probability of reaching the fractured core first is one half, lie near site-PMF maxima, although configurations at equal bond length retain different fracture probabilities. Multiple fractures remain negligible near coexistence through at least $N=50$. The framework could supply state-dependent rates to mesoscopic fracture models of polymer networks.
item.dc:creator: Aristotelis P. Sgouros

item.title: Skyrmion gears: translation-to-rotation conversion of skyrmion clusters along periodic substrates
item.description: arXiv:2610.17102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how the translational motion of a compact skyrmion cluster can be converted into collective rotation through interactions with a periodic obstacle substrate. Using an effective particle model, we consider a seven-skyrmion cluster driven along a one-dimensional array of repulsive obstacle sites. For suitable obstacle spacings and interaction strengths, repeated interactions with the substrate produce coherent clockwise or counterclockwise rotation, giving rise to gear-like cluster dynamics. We characterize these states using the translational velocity, Hall angle, angular velocity, structural deformation, and a dimensionless gear ratio that relates cluster rotation to motion over the substrate periodicity. Dynamical phase diagrams identify rotating, nonrotating, wall-guided, transverse, and deformed regimes. We further show that coherent rotation persists in the overdamped limit, demonstrating that the conversion mechanism does not require an intrinsic Magnus force and may therefore extend to other driven cluster systems, including colloidal assemblies. These results provide a simple route for controlling collective rotation through structured substrates.
item.dc:creator: N. P. Vizarim, C. J. O. Reichhardt, C. Reichhardt

item.title: Machine-learned topological transport of magnetic colloids
item.description: arXiv:2610.17344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By modulating the orientation of a uniform magnetic field it is possible to transport magnetic microparticles above magnetic patterns. In periodic patterns, driving control loops that wind around special orientations, which are dictated by the symmetry of the pattern, induce transport by one unit cell. The transport is topologically protected with trajectories controlled by the winding numbers of the control loop around the special orientations. In non-periodic patterns, the special orientations are position dependent, precluding a global characterization of the transport using a small set of winding numbers. We use here a reinforcement learning agent trained with Brownian dynamics simulation data that uses the local environment of the magnetic pattern to decide an action over the control loop. The agent autonomously discovers topological transport protocols directly from the particle response without prior characterization of the magnetic potential landscape. An agent trained solely on a complex non-periodic pattern directly generalizes to completely unseen periodic, quasicrystalline, and disordered substrates. Moreover, the agent dynamically adjusts the control loop to transport particles across lattice defects and to counterbalance external drift forces that would cause static topological loops to fail. By adding a pathfinding algorithm to the model, we additionally achieve simultaneous, independent transport of multiple identical colloids along different on demand trajectories. We demonstrate that the control loops can be directly transferred to an experimental setup to successfully drive magnetic microparticles across a non-uniform magnetic thin film.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Wohlrab, Aneena Rinu Perayil, Piotr Ku\'swik, Maciej Urbaniak, Feliks Stobiecki, Arne J. Vereijken, Arno Ehresmann, Thomas M. Fischer, Daniel de las Heras

item.title: Meso-scale modeling of cohesive cavitation in polymer networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.17360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cavitation influences the failure of elastomers and soft adhesives, but connecting its microscopic initiation to subsequent cavity growth remains challenging. Here, we develop a discrete mesoscale framework that combines finitely extensible, breakable strands with local van der Waals interactions to examine how cohesion and network heterogeneity transform distributed dilation into localized damage. In the simulations, local cohesive instability produces a network-scale precursor whose subsequent expansion is coupled to strand stretching and rupture. Cohesive strength and intrinsic defect size govern the critical hydrostatic tension, while cohesion also controls the number and spatial distribution of cavities. Under confined loading, decreasing the layer thickness promotes multiple cavities and distributed strand rupture, extending the load-bearing response and increasing the critical work density of rupture. An energetic interpretation based on the thickness dependence of the crack-driving force connects these observations to competition between additional cavity nucleation and propagation of existing damage. The results link local cohesive instability to the collective evolution of cavities and rupture in disordered polymer networks.
item.dc:creator: Saleh Assadi, Zachary T. White, Fay Salmon, Nitin Hansoge, Zhuonan Liu, Victor Crespo-Cuevas, Jason Clapper, Nikolaos Bouklas, Franck J. Vernerey

item.title: Evolution of dense liquid marbles under light tapping
item.description: arXiv:2610.18074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liquid marbles interface is composed by a dense network of grains trapped by capillarity at their surface. The mix of capillarity and granular character make their interfaces remarkable, allowing non wetting, high mobility and strong robustness which are a basis for numerous applications. A canonical experiment showing out of equilibrium nature of granular material is the so called tapping experiment, where a dry granular medium under vertical vibration reorganize an evolve toward a denser final state function of the vibration amplitude In this paper we explore the out of equilibrium nature of densely covered liquid marbles by measuring their shape, compaction and stresses evolution under vertical vibration. We show that liquid marble do indeed reorganize when submitted to taps, leading to higher internal pressure and lower effective surface tension.
item.dc:creator: Amaelle Sprocq, Th\'eo Dhoudain, Alexis Duchesne, Guillaume Lagubeau

item.title: Ionic gradients shape the spatial organization and dynamics of supramolecular polymers
item.description: arXiv:2610.18357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Living supramolecular materials such as microtubules and actin filaments assemble and function in dynamic, heterogeneous environments, subject to chemical concentration gradients. Their rapid and precise response to such gradients---via aggregation, disassembly, or autonomous motion---underlies the fine spatiotemporal control typical of living systems. Reproducing such responsiveness in synthetic materials is a central challenge in materials science and requires a molecular-level understanding of how gradients couple to supramolecular structure and dynamics, which remains difficult to access experimentally. To this end, we combine implicit-solvent coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) with the constant chemical potential MD (C${\mu}$MD) technique to investigate, at molecular resolution, the coupling of two prototypical supramolecular polymer models with externally imposed ionic concentration gradients. Despite their contrasting responses to homogeneous ionic conditions, both systems undergo pronounced spatial reorganization under the gradient, generating regions of locally enhanced supramolecular activity that are inaccessible to homogeneous systems with the same overall content of self-assembling species. Crucially, the local supramolecular dynamics is largely determined by the local concentrations, consistent with the formation of local quasi-equilibria: this direct connection between spatial composition and supramolecular activity emerges as a common governing principle across the two models. These findings shed light on the spatially complex supramolecular response that can be triggered by chemical gradients, and show how a single gradient simulation can encode this response across a continuous range of local chemical environments, thus providing a general strategy to investigate and design materials operating under spatially heterogeneous conditions.
item.dc:creator: Claudio Perego, Annalisa Cardellini, Andrea Tagliabue, Giovanni M. Pavan

item.title: Curie-Weiss cell fluid model: Fitting to experimental critical-point data
item.description: arXiv:2610.18411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine how the Curie--Weiss cell fluid model can be quantitatively related to real fluids by determining its microscopic parameters from experimental critical-point data for water, carbon dioxide, and three polyol ester lubricants (POE5, POE7, and POE9). The microscopic parameters of the model are determined from the experimental values of the critical temperature and critical density: the global attraction coupling constant is fixed by the critical temperature, and the cell volume by the critical density. The critical pressure then follows as an independent model prediction, deviating from experimental values by 10--41$\%$ across the studied substances. Varying the ratio of local repulsion to global attraction $f=J_2/J_1$ over a wide range has only a weak effect on this deviation. For $f\geq1$, the model's critical compressibility factor lays within a narrow range $Z_c\approx0.382-0.386$, remaining close to the mean-field van der Waals value $Z_c=3/8=0.375$ and consistently overestimating experimental values. The best agreement with experiment is obtained for the polyol ester lubricants and improves along the POE5--POE7--POE9 series with increasing molar mass, suggesting that multiple-occupancy cell fluid models are well suited to systems of large molecules, particularly soft-matter systems with bounded interaction potentials. We further show that generalizing the model by introducing a temperature- and phase-dependent effective attraction allows it to describe a triple point and to reproduce the broad range of critical-to-triple temperature ratios $T_c/T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ characteristic of real fluids.
item.dc:creator: I. V. Pylyuk, O. A. Dobush, M. P. Kozlovskii, R. V. Romanik, M. A. Shpot

item.title: Quantitative Modelling of Solvation in 2D Materials via Alchemical Decoupling and Potential Energy Surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.18490v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding why 2D materials remain suspended in solutions is essential to understanding the mechanisms of aggregation and exfoliation. These dynamics have been difficult to model because of the long timescales and large activation energies involved in these simulations. Here we describe an improved strategy for modelling the solvation and stability of 2D materials that uses the Gibbs free energy of solvation to accurately calibrate two disconnected potential energy surfaces for the fully desolvated and fully solvated 2D materials. By joining these surfaces using solvation energy, we obtain predictions for 2D material stability in various solvents that are qualitatively different than prior simulations and that have excellent agreement with experimental results. Our approach predicts a much higher barrier to full desolvation of the material, suggesting that materials that appear to be aggregated in fact still retain monolayers of solvent between adjacent layers of 2D materials. This work provides much needed understanding on the interactions between the solvent and 2D material that can guide future experimental work.
item.dc:creator: Lindsey N. Ioos, Duncan A. Peterson, Scott C. Warren

item.title: Extending the mean first-passage-time formalism to the reconstruction of high free-energy barriers: A top-start approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.18653v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rare events, such as crystal nucleation in mildly supercooled liquids, are characterized by waiting times that can be much longer than the timescale of the underlying microscopic dynamics. The mean first-passage time (MFPT) formalism [J. Wedekind and D. Reguera, J. Phys. Chem. B 112, 11060 (2008)] provides a route to reconstruct one-dimensional free-energy profiles from the MFPT and steady-state distribution measured along a reaction coordinate, but conventional implementations become inefficient for sufficiently high barriers because spontaneous crossings are rarely observed. We introduce a "top-start" extension that initiates trajectories near the barrier top and reconstructs the free-energy profile from their subsequent evolution away from the barrier toward lower-free-energy regions. We establish the equivalence between the top-start and two-region constructions using a Markov-chain transition-matrix formulation. We validate the method using one-dimensional random-walk simulations across low, medium, and high free-energy barriers, with transition-matrix calculations providing an exact benchmark for the corresponding discretized models. The top-start reconstruction remains accurate in the high-barrier regime where conventional MFPT sampling becomes prohibitively inefficient.
item.dc:creator: Ying Jiang, Ivan Saika-Voivod

item.title: Controlling inertial active Brownian motion via stochastic resetting
item.description: arXiv:2602.21134v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inertia is intrinsic to many living and synthetic active systems, from animals and robotic agents to colloidal swimmers, and it strongly shapes transport. Many such systems employ intermittent restart protocols to regulate exploration. Stochastic resetting provides a theoretical framework for these strategies and a route to control nonequilibrium steady states, yet the role of inertia in reset-controlled active dynamics remains poorly understood. Here we study an inertial active Brownian particle in two dimensions under complete and partial stochastic resetting. We derive exact stationary second- and fourth-order scalar moments for the different protocols wherever their stationary limits exist, and obtain the full transient evolution of the mean-squared velocity and displacement under complete resetting. Under complete resetting, inertia strongly enhances localization: at large reset rates, the steady-state mean-squared displacement decays as $r^{-3}$, rather than following the overdamped scaling $r^{-1}$. Kurtosis-based phase diagrams reveal strongly non-Gaussian position and velocity statistics, including activity-induced re-entrant behavior as a function of reset rate and inertia. The transient solutions show that resetting shifts the velocity-relaxation rates, whereas the terminal relaxation of the displacement is governed solely by the mean resetting time $1/r$, with inertia controlling the faster transient modes. Comparing complete resetting with the partial protocols, we find that resetting the velocity together with the position substantially enhances localization. Resetting the orientation to a fixed or a random direction drives the mean-squared velocity toward opposite limits. These results establish inertia, reset frequency, and the choice of reset variables as coupled control parameters for localization, relaxation, and non-Gaussian fluctuations in active systems.
item.dc:creator: Manish Patel, Amir Shee

item.title: Chapman-Enskog expansion for chirally colliding disks
item.description: arXiv:2602.21367v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a two-dimensional gas of hard disks undergoing chiral, energy- and momentum-conserving collisions. We propose a simple chiral collision rule and show that it can effectively capture collisions of spinning noncircular particles without retaining spin or orientation as kinetic variables. Despite the microscopic breaking of time-reversal symmetry, the H-theorem is obeyed, guaranteeing relaxation towards equilibrium in the absence of external forces. A Chapman-Enskog expansion yields analytical expressions for the shear and odd viscosity and the thermal conductivity. Theoretical predictions are confirmed by nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations
item.dc:creator: Ruben Lier, Pawe{\l} Matus

item.title: Unambiguous characterization of in-plane dielectric response in nanoconfined liquids: water as a case study
item.description: arXiv:2604.00700v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The in-plane dielectric constant of nanoconfined water has attracted growing interest in recent years. Nevertheless, assigning a bulk-like dielectric constant to a molecularly thin film is convention dependent because it requires choosing an effective water width. We propose the in-plane 2D polarizability, $\alpha_{\parallel}$, as a macroscopic characterization of the in-plane dielectric response that avoids this choice. Using classical molecular dynamics simulations, we compute $\alpha_{\parallel}$ via two independent and consistent methods: based on fluctuation--dissipation theory, and from the induced dipole moment when water is placed in a capacitor. Our results provide the framework to quantify the in-plane dielectric response of polar liquids across simulations and experiments.
item.dc:creator: Jon Zubeltzu

item.title: Dynamics of ring polymer melts: Memory function approach
item.description: arXiv:2605.26905v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigated the static and dynamic properties of a Rouse ring polymer modified by introducing an effective, spherically symmetric, attractive potential of entropic nature and a memory function describing the effect of dynamic entanglement. Renormalized Rouse formalism is used to approximate the time dependence of the memory matrix. The results obtained are in good agreement with existing experimental data and the results of computer simulations of ring polymer ring with , , where N_e is the number of Kuhn segments in linear polymer melts between neighboring entanglements and , the number of Kuhn segments. For large molecular weights, a refined self-consistent approximation is proposed to describe the time dependence of the memory function. It is shown that this approximation allows us to describe an exponential decrease in the self-diffusion coefficient with molecular weight of the rings, i.e., the effect of dynamic localization.
item.dc:creator: Nail Fatkullin, Carlos Mattea, Kevin Lindt, Siegfried Stapf, Margarita Kruteva

item.title: Effects of Charge Regulation on the Conformations and Dynamics of a Polyelectrolyte during Nanoparticle Adsorption
item.description: arXiv:2609.03587v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Customizing the surface characteristics and stimuli-responsive behavior of polyelectrolyte (PE) during interaction with nanoparticles (NP) have potential applications ranging from biological interactions to advanced diagnostic technologies. Using numerical simulations, we investigate how charge regulation (CR) shapes the conformation, dynamics and adsorption of PE on a oppositely charged NP and compared the results with constant charge (CC) conditions. At low solvent ion concentrations, CR barely affects the adsorption fraction, while significantly enhancing the dynamical response of the PE. However, at high ion concentrations, while complexation is suppressed in the CC case, the CR environment helps to overcome the energy barriers related to Debye screening and thermal fluctuations, thereby promoting the adsorption. By maintaining the strong PE-NP electrostatic interaction, PE exhibits a more directed ballistic-like dynamics towards NP during adsorption, in comparison to the diffusive and sub-diffusive behavior observed in the CC case. Our results emphasize that in high ion concentrations, with a strong Debye screening effect, a small fraction of charge-fluctuating sites suffices for adsorption to happen. A tunable CR mechanism is thus an efficient and robust strategy to control the biomolecular interaction and stability in complex environments.
item.dc:creator: Kawaljeet Kaur, Rashmi Kandari, Sunita Kumari, Subhajit Paul

item.title: Active fluctuations drive inertia-free absolute negative mobility in soft and living matter
item.description: arXiv:2603.06070v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Absolute negative mobility (ANM) is one of the most paradoxical transport phenomena in which a setup moves on average in a direction opposite to the applied force. The simplest system exhibiting this effect in minimal one-dimensional dynamics involves an inertial particle subjected to a constant bias while dwelling in a nonlinear, symmetric periodic potential in a nonequilibrium, nonstationary state generated by external driving. The necessity of inertia poses a significant conceptual barrier in predicting the ANM in a microscopic world of soft and living matter such as biological cells. In this work, we solve a two-decade old puzzle and demonstrate that none of the previously thought factors required for this effect are decisive. We show that the ANM may occur in a system composed of an overdamped particle in a piecewise linear symmetric periodic potential in an equilibrium state, provided that it is additionally driven by active fluctuations in the form of white Poisson shot noise. Our result may help to explain exotic transport behaviour emerging in biological cells where dynamics is typically overdamped and assisted by active fluctuations derived from various metabolic activities. It can also be exploited for effective separation strategies in a microscopic world, thus transforming fluctuations from a nuisance into a functional resource.
item.dc:creator: K. Bia{\l}as, P. H\"anggi, J. Spiechowicz

item.title: Odd stochastic density functional theory
item.description: arXiv:2609.32080v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Stochastic density functional theory (SDFT) provides a powerful framework for studying the dynamics of many-body systems both in and out of equilibrium. In its standard form, it can be viewed as a density-based formulation of coupled Langevin equations with white noise. Here, we extend SDFT to a class of systems, ranging from magnetized electrolytes to chiral active matter, that possess a chiral overdamped limit in which a relaxation timescale and an oscillation period are simultaneously taken to zero. We derive this formulation, which we dub ``odd SDFT", by taking the overdamped limit of a fluctuating hydrodynamic description of underdamped particles subject to a Lorentz force. We establish the validity and utility of the resulting framework by calculating the collective mobility tensor of interacting particles using both direct linear response and a Green-Kubo relation. We then apply the theory to the Hall conductivity of electrolytes in magnetic fields. Going beyond mean-field theory and using two distinct Green-Kubo relations, we derive the full conductivity tensor, extending the relaxation part of the Debye-H\"uckel-Onsager theory to the case of finite magnetic fields.
item.dc:creator: Yael Avni, Michel Fruchart, David Martin, Tali Khain, Vincenzo Vitelli

item.title: Directional Control of Droplet Motion via Geometric Gating
item.description: arXiv:2609.38654v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We explore new methods for inducing the movement of water droplets on elastomeric substrates, such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Our approach builds upon the well-known phenomenon that water droplets move easily across these substrates when swelled w,ith silicone oil. While designing shallow open channels and traps on a PDMS film offers a simple way to control a droplet's trajectory by tilting the substrate in two orthogonal directions, this method is poorly suited for manipulating multiple droplets simultaneously. To address this limitation, we introduce two new methods. The first method utilizes a plano-concave PDMS platform with a radius of curvature significantly larger than the size of the droplet and its translation distance. When the system's configuration is altered, this curved substrate consistently guides the droplet along a curved geodesic. The second method incorporates diode-like gates on the PDMS. These gates are created on either flat or plano-concave PDMS films by embedding thin, rigid plates into the elastomer prior to crosslinking, followed by swelling in silicone oil. This process generates sigmoidal steps that restrict droplet motion to a single direction. Finally, we demonstrate how combining these two strategies enables various forms of directed motion for both single and multiple droplets.
item.dc:creator: Manoj K. Chaudhury, Vanessa Elias, Michelle Fruge

item.title: Reference-Measure Freedom of the Effective Hamiltonian: From Stochastic Thermodynamics to the Macroscopic Limit
item.description: arXiv:2609.38994v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The effective Hamiltonian (EH), also referred to as the potential of mean force or free-energy landscape, is widely used to describe equilibrium properties and slow dynamics in chemical and soft-matter systems. However, the conventional EH has been argued to be ill-defined because it does not transform as a scalar under coordinate transformations. We identify an implicit change of reference measure (gauge), rather than the coordinate transformation itself, as the origin of this apparent problem. We formulate the EH as a scalar relative to a chosen gauge and derive the intrinsic, gauge-independent Fokker--Planck equation (FPE) on the manifold of slow variables. The conventional EH and the diffusion-dependent EH introduced in a Riemannian formulation, together with their corresponding FPEs, are thus different gauge representations of the same equilibrium measure and intrinsic stochastic dynamics. We further demonstrate that the gauge choice has an operational meaning: different restraint protocols select different reference measures. In the macroscopic limit, the leading EH becomes gauge independent within a class of subleading gauges and is determined by the large-deviation rate function. In the same limit, the stochastic dynamics reduces to gauge-independent deterministic dynamics.

item.title: Nematic order in monomer-dimer models of Heilmann and Lieb with lateral attraction in dimensions $d\ge 2$
item.description: arXiv:2610.08600v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the $d$-dimensional generalization of Models II ($d=2$) and V ($d=3$) for liquid crystals introduced by Heilmann--Lieb (1979), which consists of dimers on the hypercubic lattice at chemical potential $\mu$, interacting via a hard-core repulsion and a lateral attraction between parallel dimers with coupling constant $b>0$. For $d\in\{2,3\}$, these models were conjectured to exhibit liquid-crystalline order at low temperatures provided that $\mu+2(d-1)b>0$. We establish nematic order for all $d\ge 2$ under the additional condition $(4d-6)b>\mu$, which corresponds to the physical regime in which misaligned dimers are rare on scales comparable to the correlation length of the one-dimensional reference system. While the treatment of orientational order here follows the approach of our recent work on Model I, the proof of the absence of translational order relies on a custom implementation of cluster swapping in the sense of Sheffield (2005). Consequently, we deduce uniqueness of Gibbs measure and anisotropic exponential decay of correlations within each oriented phase.
